messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a 25-year-old nurse who came to treatment months after leaving a war zone where, as a civilian, she had spent prolonged periods trapped among the injured and the dead. Before coming to the United States she had helped in makeshift treatment areas when shelling hit her neighborhood, and the scene that returns most often is not a single detached image but a whole sensory moment that takes her over. She can still see herself kneeling on a dirty floor, trying to compress a wound while people shouted around her and another blast sounded nearby. What breaks through most painfully is the look on the face of a young woman she could not save. When the memory comes, Amina does not experience it as something finished and past; she feels, in her words, as if she is “right back there,” with the same rush of terror and helplessness in her body. The recall quickly becomes unbearable, flooding her with grief so intense that she has to shut it down.

In the weeks and months afterward, those returns of memory began to shape how she thought about herself. Each time she was pulled back into that scene and felt again how overwhelmed and unable to do enough she had been, she came away more certain that what happened had exposed something shameful about her. She had come to believe that she was inadequate, that a capable person would have done more, endured more, saved more. The grief attached itself to a deeper judgment: not only had she failed in an impossible situation, but the event had revealed that there was something fundamentally wrong with her. She spoke about this with a bowed posture and obvious reluctance, saying she felt permanently humiliated by what she had lived through, as if surviving while others died had marked her in a way other people would see if they looked closely enough.

Those beliefs began to govern how she managed her days. Because she felt defective and exposed, Amina avoided talking about the war with her boyfriend, with coworkers, and even with relatives who knew where she had been. When people asked careful questions, she gave clipped answers or changed the subject, already bracing for the shame she expected to feel if she put the memories into words. She also tried not to think about it when she was alone. If her mind edged toward the treatment room, the blood, or the face of the woman who died, she would push herself into a kind of private mental distance, drifting off into fantasies and imagined scenes that had nothing to do with her life. She described it less as comfort than as disappearing for a while, a way to avoid contact with the version of herself she now despised.

At work as a nurse, this pattern had become especially visible. A trauma page overhead, the metallic smell of blood, or the sight of a young female patient crying on a gurney could bring the war back with such force that for a few seconds she felt transported, her chest tightening as though the bombardment were happening again. The grief and overwhelm came so fast that she would have to turn away internally. She found reasons to leave the room, kept conversations strictly procedural, and afterward stared at the medication cart while her mind floated elsewhere, trying not to think at all. The more vividly the memory arrived, the more urgently she retreated from it into silence, blankness, and fantasy.

Over time, those strategies seemed to make the memories more jagged rather than less. Because Amina cut them off the moment they surfaced, they kept returning in the same raw form, with no sense of distance or completion. A brief reminder during a shift could set off the whole scene again, and each return landed with the same emotional force, as if nothing had been processed or laid to rest. In that way her efforts not to think, not to speak, and to mentally drift away left the memories poised to break back in on her, vivid and overwhelming. And when they did, they renewed the same conclusions about herself: that she was weak, deficient, and indelibly shamed by what had happened.

This had begun to affect her relationship as well as her work. Her boyfriend told her she seemed absent even when she was sitting beside him, and Amina knew he meant the moments when she vanished into her own head rather than risk talking about where she had gone emotionally. She finally sought help after a shift in which a patient’s cries abruptly pulled her back into the war, and she had to step off the unit and lock herself in a bathroom, shaking and grieving as if the loss had just occurred. What frightened her most was not only the memories themselves, but the conviction that they proved who she really was. What she hopes for, cautiously, is some way to remember without being overtaken and some chance of no longer feeling that the worst thing that happened to her is the truest thing about her.
